questions.q: How would you use the drop-down menus in SPSS to generate a frequency table?
questions.explanation: In SPSS, to generate a frequency table, navigate to **Analyze → Descriptive Statistics → Frequencies**. This opens the Frequencies dialog where you can select variables and produce frequency output.
options: Open the Output Viewer and click: Save As; Pie Chart
Click on: Analyze; Descriptive Statistics; Frequencies
Open the Variable Viewer and recode the value labels

questions.q: The command that allows reverse coding and makes data entry much more efficient in SPSS is:
questions.explanation: **Value Labels** in SPSS allow you to assign text labels to numeric codes (e.g., 1 = Male, 2 = Female), enabling reverse coding and making data entry significantly more efficient.

questions.q: How is a variable name different from a variable label in SPSS?
questions.explanation: In SPSS, a **variable name** is a short identifier (max 64 characters, no spaces) used internally, while a **variable label** is a longer, more descriptive text that appears in output to clarify what the variable represents.
options: It is longer and more detailed.
It refers to codes rather than variables.
It is shorter and less detailed.

questions.q: When should the type of measure (nominal, ordinal, scale) be defined in SPSS?
questions.explanation: The measurement level should **always** be defined in SPSS regardless of variable type, because SPSS uses this information to determine appropriate statistical procedures and chart types automatically.
options: When you intend to graph nominal variables
When you intend to graph ordinal variables
When you intend to graph interval variables

questions.q: How would you use the drop-down menus in SPSS to generate a histogram? *(Method 1)*
questions.explanation: One way to generate a histogram in SPSS is via **Analyze → Descriptive Statistics → Frequencies → Charts → Histogram**. This embeds the histogram request within the Frequencies procedure.
options: Open the Output Viewer and click: Save As; Pie Chart
Click on: Analyze; Descriptive Statistics; Frequencies; Charts; Histogram
Open the Variable Viewer and recode the value labels

questions.q: How would you use the drop-down menus in SPSS to generate a histogram? *(Method 2)*
questions.explanation: A second way to generate a histogram in SPSS is directly through **Graphs → Legacy Dialogs → Histogram**, which provides a dedicated histogram dialog independent of the Frequencies procedure.
options: Open the Output Viewer and click: Save As; Pie Chart
Click on: Analyze; Descriptive Statistics; Frequencies
Click on: Graphs; Legacy Dialogs; Histogram
Open the Variable Viewer and recode the value labels

questions.q: SPSS uses the term **'Scale'** to refer to which level(s) of data?
questions.explanation: In SPSS, the measurement level **Scale** encompasses both **interval** and **ratio** level data — i.e., continuous numeric data where arithmetic operations are meaningful. Nominal and ordinal data are kept as separate categories.
options: Both nominal and ordinal level data.
Both interval and ratio level data.

questions.q: In SPSS, which view contains the definitions of each variable in your data set?
questions.explanation: **Variable View** in SPSS is where you define each variable's properties, including its name, type, width, decimals, label, value labels, missing values, and measurement level.

questions.q: In SPSS, which view is arranged in a spreadsheet format that contains variables in columns and cases in rows?
questions.explanation: **Data View** in SPSS presents the dataset in a spreadsheet grid where each **column** represents a variable and each **row** represents a case (observation).

questions.q: In SPSS, which feature allows reverse coding and makes data entry much more efficient?
questions.explanation: **Value Labels** allow you to map numeric codes to meaningful text (e.g., 1 = "Agree", 5 = "Strongly Disagree"), which supports reverse coding and streamlines data entry by letting users enter numbers instead of full text.
